items.title: Phil Woods interviewed by Monk Rowe, Delaware Water Gap, PA, November 8, 1999
items.q: Quincy Jones heard me on that tour and he was putting together, in ’57, he was putting together a band for Dizzy for the Mideast tour. And so he hired me for that.

ctx.x: Do you feel jazz is healthier today than it has been in the past?

No, not really healthier. I think it’s become — I don’t mean to paint a bleak picture — but jazz seems to have lost its cutting edge, it seems to be in a regressive mode activated © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

somehow. I mean jazz just goes on, and it’s never been so alive and well, we’ve never had so many kids playing music, and this is a positive thing. I don’t mean to negate the import of a kid picking up an instrument because if he’s got an instrument in his mouth he’s probably less liable to buy an assault rifle. I mean I think music is good. Any cutting back of funds for music education is a big mistake, which we’re also getting involved in. But the idea of jazz being alive and well, every campus has a jazz…

items.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I had 33 people... Phil Woods... Phil Woods. Okay. What’s he going to do? Ten months. We worked with Nat Cole... Phil’s written a book about all this. Phil’s a great writer.

ctx.x: But you tell me all this stuff is an accident.

. . . I owed so much money when I came back, because when I had that band over there, I was 26. I had 33 people, dogs, Charlie Parker’s ex-wife, Charlie Parker’s son Baird, Phil Woods, dogs, grandmothers, everything. I – they told us when the show closed, you’ll get – on a Thursday – you’re guaranteed transportation to Saturday. I said, “I ain’t thinking about it. We’ve got a gig at the Olympic Theatre Saturday night.” Now that’s really logical, right? And one in Sweden. So I stayed over there with 33 people for…
How are they going to get home? They believed in you.

items.title: Phil Woods — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And from that Quincy Jones heard me on that tour and he hired me for the Dizzy Gillespie band

ctx.x: They don’t teach you that in school.

They don’t teach you that at school, at Julliard, no. Or Berklee, for that matter. Even a jazz school doesn’t have that course. But the whole bus had to get, I mean the these cats, Basie's band would get their itinerary and it could be, they were six-week tours, eight- week tours, they’d go out for a while, you know. This tour was a long tour, we went everywhere and they could tell you where they were going to be eating, where they were going to be sleeping, who they were going to be sleeping with, where they’re…

“Sweet Lorraine,” which was Dizzy’s wife’s name, and here comes Dizzy on a baggage cart. They threw down like a rope ladder and he clambered up and off we went. Our first stop, we stopped in Baghdad for gas and then our first gig was in Abadan, Iran, where they do all the oil, I mean we could hear we could hear in Iran we could hear they were shooting each other in Iraq right across the river, they were, even then back in ‘56, that was going on, ‘57. And uh yeah, that was, we went to we went to Beirut, we went to…
